summary: This document defines a TACACS+ client YANG module that augments the System Management data model of RFC 7317, so devices can use TACACS+ servers for centralized authentication, authorization and accounting. It does not endorse the security mechanisms of TACACS+ itself. It was replaced by RFC 9950.

eli5.summary: Network gear can ask a central server who may log in. This document defines the settings form for that on a device. It was replaced by RFC 9950.

questions: how to configure tacacs+ with yang
subtitle: How network devices configure centralized authentication with TACACS+.

tldr.problem: Network devices need a standard way to configure TACACS+ servers for centralized user authentication, authorization and accounting, but there was no standard data model for this.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9105 defines a YANG module that extends the System Management data model (RFC 7317) with configuration options for TACACS+ client settings, including server addresses, ports, shared secrets, timeout values and statistics.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now configure TACACS+ authentication in a standard way using network management protocols like NETCONF and RESTCONF, but this RFC was replaced by RFC 9950.

today: RFC 9105 was a Proposed Standard published in August 2021. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9950, which supersedes it with updated content.

sections.title: Centralized Authentication on Network Devices
sections.content:
Network devices like routers and switches need to authenticate users who log in to administer them. Instead of storing local usernames and passwords on each device, administrators can use a centralized TACACS+ server to handle authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) for the entire network.

TACACS+ is defined in RFC 8907. RFC 7317 defined a YANG data model for system management that included support for local users and RADIUS servers. RFC 9105 extends that model to add support for TACACS+ configuration, so devices can be configured using standard network management tools.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing down each person's password on every device, a central server keeps track of who can log in where.

sections.title: The TACACS+ Data Model Structure
sections.content:
The YANG module adds a tacacs-plus container to the system data model. Under it is a list of server entries, each defining a TACACS+ server that the device can use.

Each server entry contains the server's address and port, a shared secret for authentication between client and server, an optional source address or interface for outbound packets, a VRF instance for routing, and settings like timeout and single-connection mode. The module also includes read-only statistics counters for each server, tracking connection attempts, messages sent and received, and sessions completed.
sections.eli5: The settings list says: this is server number one at this address, use this secret, wait this long for a reply, and count how many times we talk to it.

sections.title: Server Parameters
sections.content:
Each TACACS+ server must have a server-type field indicating whether it provides authentication, authorization, accounting or any combination of the three. The address field holds the server's hostname or IP address, and the port defaults to port 49 if not specified.

The shared-secret is a string known to both client and server; RFC 9105 recommends it be at least 32 characters long with mixed character types for security. The timeout field (default 5 seconds) controls how long the device waits for a response before trying another server. The single-connection boolean allows multiple AAA sessions to reuse a single TCP connection for efficiency.
sections.eli5: Tell the device: use this server at this address, wait 5 seconds for answers, use this secret to talk to it safely.

sections.title: Using the Model with NETCONF and RESTCONF
sections.content:
YANG data models are designed to be used with network management protocols. The YANG module can be accessed and configured using NETCONF (Network Configuration Protocol) or RESTCONF (RESTful interface to NETCONF).

NETCONF uses SSH for secure transport, while RESTCONF uses HTTPS. Both support the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM), which restricts what different users are allowed to read and modify. The sensitive shared-secret leaf is protected with default-deny-all access control, requiring explicit permission to read or write it.
sections.eli5: A network manager connects to the device over SSH or HTTPS and says 'set up this TACACS+ server,' and the device handles it.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Write access to the TACACS+ server list is sensitive, because an attacker who can modify it could point the device to a rogue authentication server and gain control. The shared-secret leaf is especially sensitive and is protected by the NACM default-deny-all restriction.

RFC 9105 notes that the security of TACACS+ itself depends on protecting the shared secret from disclosure. TACACS+ does not use encryption, only obfuscation, so the shared secret and all traffic between client and server should only travel over a secure network or through a secure tunnel.
sections.eli5: If a hacker changes the server settings, they can trick the device into asking a fake server for passwords. So only trusted people are allowed to change these settings.
